title: Money mule red flags: how to spot mule accounts
summary: A mule account looks ordinary until you look at how money moves through it and who holds it. The account patterns investigators describe, how mules are…
body_markdown:
The FBI defines a money mule as someone who transfers or moves illegally acquired money on behalf of someone else. Mules receive money that often came from victims of fraud and pass it on, through bank transfers, cash withdrawals, cryptocurrency or prepaid cards, which puts distance between the victims and the people who profit. Some mules know what they are doing, and others are recruited through fake jobs or online relationships and do not.


In the account: money that passes straight through, deposits from several people with no link to each other, and quick cash withdrawals, cryptocurrency purchases or onward transfers, often out of line with the customer's history. In the holder: an identity with no past, a remote job moving payments for a company that cannot be found, and an employer or contact details shared with other new accounts. No single sign settles it, so research the holder before deciding what the account is.


Often through job offers that involve receiving and passing on money, such as remote money transfer agent roles, posted on job sites and social media or sent by direct message, and through online romances and friendships. Europol names newcomers to a country, unemployed people, students and people in economic hardship among the most targeted, says the most likely targets are under 35, and reports that some groups have begun recruiting people aged 12 to 21. The FBI says anyone can be approached.


The FBI describes unwitting mules, who are unaware they are part of a scheme, witting mules, who ignore obvious red flags, and complicit mules, who know their role and may open many accounts or recruit others. Some mule accounts are opened with someone else's personal details or with fake documents. People can move between types, and some start as victims of the same fraudsters they later work for.


Be wary of any job that asks you to receive money into your own bank account and send it on, or to open an account or register a company for the work. Other signs listed by the FBI, the Secret Service and Europol are duties with no clear description, a commission for moving money, an employer writing from a free email address and a recruiter who will not appear on camera. Look the company up in the business registry it names, and search its name with the words scam, review or complaint.


Explain what the job or relationship really is and pass on the advice the Justice Department and Europol give: stop moving money, stop talking to the person giving directions, do not send that person any money still held, tell the bank and report it. Follow your own procedures for the account, report the recruiter's advert to the platform that hosts it, and in the US file a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center. In the Money Mule Initiative whose results the Justice Department announced in May 2024, about 2,970 of the more than 3,000 actions against mules were warning letters.
